items.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002
items.q: Look at Tommy Flanagan. I grew up with Tommy and Barry and Kenny Burrell and we are all very close.

ctx.x: Okay. Was there a Detroit sound? Do you think there is a Detroit sound?

Woooah, yeah. We’re all originals. I mean most of them. Look at Tommy Flanagan. I grew up with Tommy and Barry and Kenny Burrell and we are all very close. And our hero at the time, from Detroit, was Hank Jones and Milt Jackson. Because Milt Jackson had gone off with Dizzy Gillespie and Hank Jones had been out there for a while, even though he wasn’t originally from Detroit. So we had our own — we were struggling with this music, you know, going around. I should say I was struggling with it. Because the prejudice…

items.title: Sheila Jordan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I remember one time with Tommy Flanagan. I was quite young. I don‟t remember where we were. But I wanted to do If You Could See Me Now. And he said, uh, “What key?”

ctx.x: Yeah, pitch problems. How, how do you negotiate that? How are you able to still encourage [inaudible/overlapping]?

Well… I say go to a voice teacher. I‟m not a voice teacher, you know. And uh, that… one of my things is go to a voice teacher and see if there can‟t be some kinda exercises that you can take that keep your pitch together. „Cause I know I have had singers whose pitch is… and, you know, but I don‟t make it ultra obvious in front of everybody. And I do it in a very loving, nurturing way, because you have to… I don‟t know about instrumentalists, but I know singers are very sensitive. And the minute that they feel…

like that, you know. And they‟re very appreciative and, and they really, they really enjoy that. They really get something out of that. I‟ve had many, many letters and cards and thank you notes. Not to brag, but I‟m just saying, it must work, whatever I‟m doing. I don‟t know. But it must work. I‟m teaching them how I learned it and I had to fall on my face to know what I wanted, you know. And I had to. I took a lot of, oh, falls. Heavy falls. Not knowing how to talk down a tune or what I wanted. And the reason…
